title: Alito plans to stay on Supreme Court, even if Democrats regain Senate: Report
description: Samuel Alito Jr., associate justice of the US Supreme Court, prior to an interview at the US Supreme Court in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Sept.
body: Samuel Alito Jr., associate justice of the US Supreme Court, prior to an interview at the US Supreme Court in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Al Drago | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSupreme Court Justice Samuel Alito plans to remain on the court through at least next summer, even if Democrats regain majority control in the Senate from Republicans in November's midterm election, he said in a new report.Bloomberg reported Tuesday that Alito, 76, has ruled out retiring during the brief lame-duck session of Congress after the election, when Republicans would still hold their Senate majority through early January even if they lose control for the next Congress.If Democrats are the majority in the next Congress, they may block any Supreme Court nominee of President Donald Trump, a Republican."I intend to stick around through this term," Alito told Bloomberg, referring to the court's current term, which began Monday and which will end in late June or early July. "I made that decision many months ago," said Alito, whose first book, "So Ordered: An Originalist's View of the Constitution, the Court and Our Country," has just been published.Alito was nominated to the Supreme Court in 2005 by then-President George W. Bush, another Republican. Alito is one of six conservative justices on the nine-member court. Three of the other conservatives — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — were nominated by Trump.Bloomberg reported that Alito, in the interview, acknowledged that the idea of retiring had crossed his mind.But he also said, "I don't feel mentally or physically decrepit," according to the news outlet.In a recent interview with CBS News, Alito said he considered retiring this year."It's something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term," he told CBS.Democrats in the Senate are still stung by then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell blocking the Senate from considering the nomination by then-President Barack Obama of Merrick Garland for the Supreme Court in 2016. That block, which McConnell claimed was because there was not enough time to consider the nomination that was made in March, opened the way for Trump to appoint Gorsuch after he became president.McConnell, R-Ky., after the death of liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in September 2020 also orchestrated the swift confirmation of Coney Barrett shortly before the presidential election that year, which ended with Trump's defeat and led to President Joe Biden, a Democrat, taking office in early 2021.

schema.headline: Alito plans to stay on Supreme Court, even if Democrats regain Senate: Report

title: Russian lab worker's suspected plague death leaves experts puzzled
description: watch nowThe unexplained death of a lab technician at a Russian research institute handling plague bacteria has raised questions among infectious dise
body: watch nowThe unexplained death of a lab technician at a Russian research institute handling plague bacteria has raised questions among infectious disease experts, who say the circumstances surrounding the case are unusual and key details remain unanswered.According to local reports, some 200 people have been put under medical observation, or quarantined, in the Siberian area of Irkutsk. Other reports say an incident in the lab dealing with the bacteria preceded the fatality. CNBC has not been able to independently verify these reports.Russia told the World Health Organization on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk, according to a WHO spokesperson. It wasn't immediately clear if that included the diseased lab worker. While the WHO and health authorities around the world say the risk of a wider outbreak appears low, experts told CNBC that the reported circumstances of the death are difficult to reconcile with the stringent safeguards normally used when working with the deadly pathogen.Javier Pizarro-Cerda, head of the Yersinia Research Unit at the Institut Pasteur in Paris, told CNBC he was "very surprised" by the report coming out of Russia, since people working with plague normally take serious protective measures because of the dangers of exposure. "You work with a full body suit. You work with masks. You work with gloves. So even if you break a tube, normally you should be protected," he said. In Russia, there's also a vaccine for plague. However, it doesn't meet the standards expected elsewhere and offers low, transient protection, Pizarro-Cerda added. A fatal diseasePlague is an often fatal disease with very rapid progression. The fatality rate of pneumonic plague is nearly 100% if left untreated, and about 50% if treated. Several experts on the Yersinia pestis bacterium that causes plague told CNBC that isolation and monitoring of anyone who had been in contact with the diseased person is a normal and sensible strategy.As for the origin of the suspected case of pneumonic plague, Yersinia pestis exists naturally in animal reservoirs, especially among rodents, but it is highly unlikely the employee would have contracted the disease elsewhere, according to Pizarro-Cerda.The person would have had to visit a very specific place, been in contact with contaminated people or a sick animal in a wild environment, said Pizarro-Cerda.Reservoirs of Yersinia pestis exist on every continent except Oceania, however, that does not mean human cases occur everywhere those reservoirs exist.  Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said the situation is under control and that measures have been implemented in response to the case. It also said that "based on the results of extensive testing, no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities were detected in the patient's sample."The WHO said in a statement to CNBC on Monday that the cause of death is still unconfirmed and testing is reportedly underway. All of the patient's contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for illness, and none to date have shown symptoms of illness, the WHO added.Key questions remainIt's not clear why dozens of people would be put under medical observation in the region if there weren't suspicions of plague exposure. According to Pizarro-Cerda, testing for plague is straightforward and quick. "If you perform an autopsy, it should be extremely easy because if it's pulmonary plague, then the lungs of the person should be filled with the bacteria," he said. Given that the death occurred on October 2, if testing had been done, authorities would have already been able to find evidence of plague if it existed.The Russian Health Ministry and Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor didn't respond to CNBC's request for further information. A European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control spokesperson said they were aware of the case of pneumonia of unknown origin in eastern Russia that is suspected to be the plague, but cautioned that "that suspicion is not yet confirmed.""The case is in Irkutsk, Siberia, close to the Russian border with Mongolia. There is little travel between Irkutsk and the EU/EEA, particularly at present due to Russia's war against Ukraine," they added. Based on currently available information, there are no reports of additional cases or sustained human-to-human transmission.As opposed to the more widely known form of plague, which affects the lymphatic system and is associated with the Black Death in the 14th century, pneumonic plague can spread from person to person. While less transmissible than, for example, the flu or Covid-19, it's still more of a concern from a disease outbreak perspective.Traditional wooden houses in the city of Irkutsk, Russia, 30 November 2016. Photo: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa | usage worldwide   (Photo by Bernd Weissbrod/picture alliance via Getty Images)Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty Images"Plague is still endemic in many parts of the world, including western parts of the U.S., [but] there shouldn't be too much concern as the transmission of Yersinia pestis between humans is generally poor," Brendan Wren, professor at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, told CNBC.Even so, "any case is alarming, especially under these circumstances," Simon Clarke, associate professor in Cellular Microbiology at the University of Reading, told CNBC. What's needed now to allow scientists to properly assess the situation is "transparency about what this person was working on and why, and what they have died of, and what they've done, where they've done it, in order to try and put a firewall around [their] contacts," he said.The U.S. State Department said they are closely monitoring the situation with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention but highlighted that many details remain unconfirmed. "We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," a spokesperson told CNBC.President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday the U.S. would do what it could to help Russia.watch nowThe working relationship between Moscow and Washington over the past five to six weeks appears to have improved, and there has been a lot of interaction between officials at different levels, according to Macro Advisory CEO Chris Weafer."In that sense, it doesn't surprise me that Trump would have made this offer to help partly to make sure this does not become another major global event that kills people and disrupts global economy," Weafer told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday."But also, it just reflects the fact that there is this good, ongoing, and what appears to be fairly constant dialog between Washington and Moscow right now on a number of issues, not least of which, of course, is about the Ukraine-Russia conflict."

title: Student riots engulf France as far-right presidential frontrunner Le Pen vows fiscal turnaround
description: Students carry out a blocking protest at the Cesar Baggio secondary school in Lille on September 29, 2026.Sameer Al-doumy | Afp | Getty ImagesMass stu
body: Students carry out a blocking protest at the Cesar Baggio secondary school in Lille on September 29, 2026.Sameer Al-doumy | Afp | Getty ImagesMass student riots are escalating across France, with the violent clashes leading to arson, severe injuries and thousands of arrests. Protests erupted late last month in Paris, spreading into a nationwide movement that has seen students blockade schools and take to the streets to voice their discontent with teacher shortages, long days and dilapidated school buildings. Hundreds of schools have remained shuttered across the country as the rallies drag on. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said Monday evening that 190 students had been injured in the protests, with a 15-year-old boy reportedly losing a hand in clashes with riot police in the northern city of Lens. France's Justice Ministry said Monday that 5,060 people had been arrested since the protests started, 87% of whom are minors. Although Geffray said in an interview last week that the movement was "legitimate at the outset," France's Interior Ministry said the unrest "no longer has anything to do with the legitimate expression of high-school students' demands."Student body L'Union Étudiante said the protests would continue in various locations across France on Tuesday. "Together, we demand resources for young people," the union said in a Sept. 29 statement, according to a Google Translation. "We call for continued mobilization and for everyone to join in all its forms: rallies, blockades, and the [upcoming] demonstration."Anti-riot police officers face protesting students carrying out blockading action outside the secondary school Le Corbusier, in Aubervilliers, northern Paris on October 1, 2026. Lou Benoist | Afp | Getty ImagesBut the French government has little fiscal headroom to allocate funding to education. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's administration is about to start tough budget negotiations against a backdrop of division and economic turmoil.Finance Minister Roland Lescure told reporters on Thursday that the 2027 budget was targeting a fiscal adjustment worth 54 billion euros ($60.7 billion). Cuts are planned to come, in part, from freezing wages for public sector workers like teachers.Previous budget deadlocks have toppled French governments in recent years. Lawmakers have 70 days to debate and amend the budget proposal submitted by Lecornu's government on Thursday — but previous governments have leaned on emergency laws to force budgets through after the politically fractured parliament failed to reach a consensus on fiscal policy. Political instability linked to the division on spending and budget cuts has put pressure on French government bonds, known as OATs, which have also been weighed down this year by a global debt sell-off and concerns about the country's finances. The benchmark French 10-year yield has risen 129 basis points this year, according to LSEG data. Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconFrance 10-year government bondThe euro has also come under pressure, with the currency falling to a 17-month low against the U.S. dollar Monday.Le Pen vows fiscal turnaround Further political instability is also expected to develop when France holds its presidential election in the spring. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, currently projected as the frontrunner in polls, said in a speech on Tuesday that "if the French people do not opt ​​for a political break with the status quo, France is heading toward a de facto default."Marine Le Pen President of the Rassemblement National RN parliamentary group and candidate in the 2027 French presidential election speaking on September 28, 2026. Bastien Ohier | Afp | Getty ImagesShe said her policies — including "the abolition of more than 120 ridiculous or unnecessary taxes," "corrections to unfair and ineffective measures within the current pension system," a cap on France's net contribution to EU budget to 5 billion euros and "combating the aggressive tax optimization strategies of multinational corporations" — would bring the overall deficit below the 3% threshold within 18 months and equal 140 billion euros in savings by 2032."This radical effort is a deliberate move to send a clear signal that the slide in public finances is over and that markets can once again view France as a reliable partner," she said.France is subject to the EU's excessive deficit procedure, with the bloc recommending the country ends its excessive deficit by 2029 — but it has a long way to go.EU treaties set reference values of 3% of GDP for government deficits and 60% for government debt. Last year, France's deficit reached 5.1% of GDP, while its debt-to-GDP ratio hit 119% by the end of June.Bond markets 'punishing France'Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group, told CNBC on Monday that Le Pen was "the most popular leader right now in France.""What she's been promising is if she becomes president she will take 120 billion euros out of the budget over the five years of her term," he said on "U.S. Markets Edition.""The only problem is she refuses to raise any taxes, she refuses to touch any major social spending, which is over 50% of the French expenditure, and she's going to bring down the pension level. So obviously she's a magician, because there's no other place this money is going to come from... if she wants to win as president, and she also wants to have a credible budget, those two things do not align."Investors trading French bonds "have figured this out," he said. "They're clearly punishing France, kind of the way they were punishing the Brits when they were saying utterly incredible things that don't work from a market perspective," Bremmer added. This week has "brought some initial signs that the pressure on France was stabilizing, with a clear outperformance in French debt," Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said in a Tuesday note. A volatile trading session on Monday saw the OAT-bund spread — the gap in French borrowing costs above Germany's — widen by 10 basis points in the morning before finishing 4.3 basis points tighter.European bond yields were widely lower on Tuesday. The German 10-year yield fell 5 basis points as the French 10-year yield tumbled 9 basis points. The bond market moves have "finally brought some respite after last week's rout, when we saw some of the biggest spread widening in years," the Deutsche Bank analysts added.Widening "spreads," the splintering in bond yield moves among euro area nations, in recent weeks has raised memories of the Sovereign Debt Crisis of the early 2010s and raised questions about whether the European Central Bank would deploy its Transmission Protection Instrument, an intervention meant only to be used to calm severely disorderly market moves.In comments reported by Reuters, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure said Tuesday that the government "must do everything to avoid getting to that point." Lescure also said it was not a lack of confidence that was causing the OAT sell-off, but fewer buyers.Ken Egan, director of sovereigns at ratings agency KBRA, said the sharp widening in OAT spreads in recent weeks — with France's 10-year yield now around 23 basis points above Italy's — reflected "both concern over the fiscal trajectory and a growing political uncertainty premium, with the market questioning how quickly a credible path to fiscal improvement can be delivered."— CNBC's Charlotte Reed contributed to this report.

title: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
description: The new business-class cabin on the Airbus A380.Courtesy: British AirwaysBritish Airways is building what it calls the "world's largest" business-clas
body: The new business-class cabin on the Airbus A380.Courtesy: British AirwaysBritish Airways is building what it calls the "world's largest" business-class cabin and ripping out dozens of coach-class seats, the starkest example yet of how airlines are betting their future on high-spending travelers.The changes are part of a massive overhaul of the British Airways fleet and its ground services, including lounges at its London Heathrow hub. Here's what's changing:British Airways will outfit its Airbus A380, the world's largest passenger plane, with a monster 106-seat business-class cabin, up from the current configuration of 97 business-class seats.First class will also be refreshed and will include 12 suites, down from the current A380 configuration of 14.Premium economy class will grow to 84 seats from 55.Standard economy seats will shrink to just 215 from 303.The new club world business-class cabin on the Airbus A380.Courtesy: British AirwaysBritish Airways said the 106 business-class suites, with sliding doors, will take up the entirety of the A380's upper deck. Airlines have been spending years and hundreds of millions of dollars to expand their pricier seats, capitalizing on demand for roomier options and travelers' appetite for more luxurious trips. British Airways' joint-venture partner, American Airlines, last month debuted a 70-seat business class on its largest Boeing aircraft. Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson told CNBC in a recent interview that customers are seeking high-end options on long flights, like its Perth-London nonstop. "There is absolutely a customer who wants this and is prepared to pay a premium for it," she said.Those more expensive seats command a premium. Even extra legroom on trips across the Atlantic can go for more than $200 per leg, with surcharges of more than $1,000 for premium economy seats after purchase. The prices can be even higher if they're selected at booking. The top-end seats regularly run $5,000 and even well over $10,000 on lengthier flights.Deliveries of new aircraft have even been delayed because some of the new seats are so elaborate that carriers have been waiting for parts or federal certification.British Airways' overhaul of the cabins on its 12 A380s is also a bet on the jumbo jet, which many carriers have retired in recent years, opting for smaller, more fuel-efficient jets. Airbus delivered the last A380 to the plane's largest user, Emirates, in late 2021.watch nowRead more about airlines' race to win over big spendersAlaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel raceBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to first-class seats and premium upgradesUnited ditches more economy seats to make room for bigger premium cabins with new layoutsCaviar and privacy: Airlines' business-class wars are hereAmerican Airlines is arriving late to the luxury travel boom. Can it catch up?First-class seats are getting so fancy they’re holding up new airplanesAirlines can’t add high-end seats fast enough as travelers treat themselves to first class

title: Why deep-red Kansas has become an unexpected Senate battleground
description: Sen. Roger Marshall, a Republican from Kansas, and Democratic U.S. senatorial candidate Adam Hamilton of Kansas.Eric Lee | Bloomberg | Getty Images Co
body: Sen. Roger Marshall, a Republican from Kansas, and Democratic U.S. senatorial candidate Adam Hamilton of Kansas.Eric Lee | Bloomberg | Getty Images Colin E. Braley | APIn a state that hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1932, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall suddenly finds himself in a competitive race with weeks to go until the 2026 midterm elections. Stubborn inflation, blowback from White House trade policies, and a formidable Democratic challenger in megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton have combined to turn ruby-red Kansas into an unexpected Senate battleground.The tightening contest has forced Marshall into a balancing act confronting a growing number of vulnerable Republicans: creating space from President Donald Trump on issues that pose risks at home without alienating his base."When a sitting Republican senator in Kansas starts running away from their leader in the White House, the five-alarm bell is ringing for the entire party," said Bob Beatty, a political scientist at Washburn University. "Loyalty to Washington is becoming a liability when voters are feeling the squeeze at home."The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted the race from "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican" on Sept. 23.A September Emerson College/Nexstar survey of 750 Kansas likely voters put Hamilton at 45% and Marshall at 43%, a dead heat within the poll's 3.6% margin of error. In the same poll, Trump's approval in Kansas stood at 40%, with 53% disapproving and nearly half of likely voters naming the economy their top issue.National Republican groups have taken note. Outside groups are now pouring millions into Kansas to defend the seat that once sat safely outside the Senate battlefield. At stake is the GOP's Senate majority.Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., waves as Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., looks on during an event with Vice President JD Vance at Webco Manufacturing in Olathe, Kansas, Sept. 14, 2026.Mark Schiefelbein | Getty ImagesEconomic squeezeMarshall has been a stalwart Trump ally for years. Though Trump carried Kansas by 16 points in 2024, the senator has recently shown a willingness to distance himself. In September, Trump threatened to ban U.S. sales of aircraft built by Canadian manufacturer Bombardier, potentially putting the future of many of the company's roughly 1,500 Wichita-based jobs in limbo. While Marshall offered little resistance to the broader trade dispute that spurred the threat, he insisted he had taken the fight for local aerospace jobs "inside the Oval Office."Meanwhile, farmers are being squeezed from both ends. Trade disputes and retaliatory tariffs have weighed on grain and soybean markets just as the Iran war has driven up fuel costs. Diesel — essential for combines, tractors and transport trucks — jumped nearly a dollar a gallon during one 30-day stretch this harvest season, according to AAA.Ranchers have been hit, too. In a bid to tamp down ground beef prices, Trump in August moved to lower tariffs on an additional 300,000 metric tons of imports for lean beef trimmings."The interference in Washington is causing more harm than good," said Matt Teagarden, chief executive of the Kansas Livestock Association. "Many of our members would prefer policymakers to let the market work." The association endorsed Marshall in both his 2016 House race and his 2020 Senate campaign. This year, it has declined to endorse either Marshall or Hamilton.Marshall, meanwhile, has offered calibrated pushback against several Trump administration policies, calling for "targeted relief" on fuel costs and arguing the administration took the wrong approach to food prices.Immigration enforcement further complicated Marshall's balancing act. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids have swept across southwestern Kansas, home to some of the nation's largest meatpacking plants and feedlots, stoking fear among immigrant workers."Workers stayed home, causing plants to shorten shifts, slow production lines or cancel shifts altogether," Teagarden told CNBC. "Canceled processing left feedlots holding cattle longer, driving up costs in an industry already facing labor shortages."Marshall responded with measured critique: "When ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement," he posted on X on Sept. 23. "Our sheriffs and police know these communities better than anyone."Adding to Marshall's troubles are controversies all his own.The New York Times reported on Sept. 8 that Marshall, a physician, sued more than 700 patients of his medical clinic over unpaid bills. The Times found that patients were arrested in 81 cases after missing court dates; lawyers also garnished patients' wages and bank accounts, and patients were routinely charged 18% annual interest.Democrats have also criticized Marshall for his ties to Florida, where he maintained a home.Marshall's campaign rejected both attacks. Brent Robertson, Marshall's chief of staff, called the premise of Hamilton's medical-debt attack "a lie on its face," noting that the Kansas Bill of Rights prohibits imprisonment for debt. He also said, "Senator Marshall lives in Kansas, and his residence on 300+ acres is well established."A Democratic challengerMarshall's tightening contest is part of a widening defensive perimeter for the GOP. Cook moved Republican-held Senate races in Texas and Iowa to "Toss Up" in August. In September, it shifted Kansas toward Democrats and moved South Carolina onto the competitive map. As of Sept. 23, the publication rates control of the Senate a toss-up.Democratic U.S. senatorial candidate Adam Hamilton of Kansas, right, visits with Health Partnership Clinic Chief Health Officer Tiffany Swanson during a tour of the medical facility for low-income families in Olathe, Kansas, Aug. 12, 2026.Colin E. Braley | AP"Nobody had Kansas on their bingo card as a battleground when this cycle began," Kansas Democratic Party Chair Jeanna Repass said.Hamilton brings unique crossover appeal to the race, political experts tell CNBC. He spent three decades building the largest United Methodist congregation in the country and entered the race with an established network reaching well beyond traditional Democratic circles."Hamilton is wildly popular in places where I can't even get a Democratic candidate to run for a House seat, a state legislative seat," Repass told CNBC, adding that Hamilton has supporters "knocking every door" in some of those communities.Hamilton's background — he has previously been registered as both a Republican and a Democrat and briefly became unaffiliated this year while considering an independent bid — has also made it easier for him to appeal outside the Democratic base, Beatty said."He creates a permission structure for moderate Republicans and independents to cross the aisle," Beatty told CNBC. That appeal is yielding endorsements from prominent former Republican Govs. Bill Graves and Mike Hayden, as well as Marshall's recent GOP primary challenger, Arch Naramore. Meanwhile, the September Emerson College poll found Hamilton leading Marshall among independent voters, 42% to 27%."Kansas isn't undergoing an ideological realignment overnight," said David Kensinger, a veteran Republican strategist and former chief of staff to Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback. "But voters are frustrated right now and Hamilton isn't the one in power."Hamilton's strategy also depends on Kansas' recent penchant for bucking GOP orthodoxy. In 2022, nearly 59% rejected an amendment that would have allowed lawmakers to further restrict abortion, then re-elected Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly three months later. In 2025, enough Republican legislators resisted Trump's push for mid-decade redistricting to block a special session. And in August, voters overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-backed proposal to change how state Supreme Court justices are selected."Kansas is still a very deep red state," Repass told CNBC. "We just have purple veins."The GOP firewallDespite the warning signs, Kansas Republicans have seen versions of this before.After Bob Dole narrowly survived reelection in the aftermath of Watergate in 1974, every Republican Senate nominee in Kansas has won by double digits. More recently, Republican Sen. Pat Roberts appeared locked in a close contest with independent Greg Orman in 2014 before winning by roughly 11 points. Six years later, Marshall's race against Democrat Barbara Bollier also appeared competitive late in the campaign before he won by more than 11 points."This has happened regularly," Kansas Republican Party Chair Danedri Herbert told CNBC. "Republicans who drift or remain undecided often return to the party as Election Day approaches."Marshall also retains a substantial financial advantage. As of July 15, the cutoff for the candidates' pre-primary FEC reports, his campaign held $5.4 million in cash, more than triple Hamilton's $1.7 million.But Republicans aren't taking chances. On Friday, the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate Republican leadership, began a multimillion-dollar advertising campaign in Kansas to support Marshall while pausing additional spending in North Carolina, Semafor reported. The group has reserved nearly $8.2 million in Kansas through Election Day, according to AdImpact."Our mission is simple: help Republicans win throughout Kansas," Herbert said. "The Senate race is too critical to take for granted, and we are treating it that way."

schema.headline: Why deep-red Kansas has become an unexpected Senate battleground

title: Meta joins with group of companies to tame ‘chaos’ of doing business with AI bots
description: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of the Facebook parent company Meta, takes the stage at the Meta Connect developer conference. Andrej Sokolow | Picture Alliance
body: Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of the Facebook parent company Meta, takes the stage at the Meta Connect developer conference. Andrej Sokolow | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesA month after Meta's launch of Muse, the personal agent that quickly turned into a viral sensation, a group of companies is coming together to try to simplify the process of bringing the technology into the business world.Meta, Walmart, Stripe and a handful of other companies are publishing what they're calling a "personal agent protocol." It's an open standard meant to dictate how artificial intelligence agents can interact with businesses.Enterprise AI startup Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, is part of the group. Taylor, who's also chairman of OpenAI and is leading the initiative, told CNBC in an interview that companies have a lot of work to do to figure out how and when personal agents are able to access information. "Companies will know when it's a personal agent versus an actual person. For a lot of companies there's a risk: you don't want just a random bot that isn't acting on behalf of a person to have access to this service," Taylor said. “It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists."Meta's Muse has become the most popular and buzzy version of personal AI agents since hitting the market in early September. It soared to the top of Apple's App Store and remains there, ahead of ChatGPT. However, Amazon is among the companies that have blocked Meta's agents, citing worries of website scraping. Amazon also blocked Perplexity's AI agent and sued the startup in November, alleging the company took steps to "conceal" its AI agents so they could continue to scrape Amazon's website without approval. Perplexity called the lawsuit a "bully tactic."For the new standard, Taylor compared it with the experience of logging into other websites with Google or Facebook credentials, technology he worked on when he was tech chief at Facebook. He said the practice will help with authentication so that businesses know if they're dealing with a bot, and will provide visibility into what personal agents are actually doing through these websites. David Singleton, vice president of engineering and consumer products at Meta Superintelligence Labs and former technology chief at Stripe, highlighted security. In order for agents to work well, he said, customers need to share credit card and personal information, and the new standard creates some level of visibility and control."We're defining rails that we hope personal agents and business agents can run over for the future," Singleton said, comparing it to email. "If you think about email, it works great because it is a standard that everyone can use to talk to each other, and we think this is going to be quite similar."Singleton said Muse already has millions of users in the U..S and it's "growing rapidly." "What we're finding is that people love using Muse for all kinds of things, things like signing their kids up for classes, finding and buying the best gifts, scheduling that dentist appointment that you have been putting off for six months," he said. "We need a mechanism to have it go faster and smoother."While OpenAI and Anthropic aren't on board now, Taylor said he expects the AI giants to participate, and indicated he will be "really disappointed" if it's not being used by competitors.  "The whole point of this is to be an open standard," Taylor said.

schema.headline: Meta joins with group of companies to tame ‘chaos’ of doing business with AI bots

title: Trump hedges on paying back government for ads that already aired
description: US President Donald Trump speaks in the East Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, Sept. 30, 2026.Jonathan Ernst | ReutersPresident Donald
body: US President Donald Trump speaks in the East Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., US, Sept. 30, 2026.Jonathan Ernst | ReutersPresident Donald Trump hedged Tuesday when asked whether he would reimburse the U.S. government for previously aired television advertisements that praised him, saying, "We'll decide."The ads cost the federal government nearly $10 million before Trump on Monday announced that he and his political action committee will pay for the segments in the face of criticism that they are propoganda and aimed at helping Republican political candidates.The White House later Monday clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service announcements going forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. The prior airings reportedly were funded from a pool of up to $20 million set aside by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.Asked whether he would reimburse the government for the costs of ads already aired, Trump told reporters, "The ads were really good.""They were promotion for the country, done by many presidents before," he said. "So we'll decide."Trump's latest comments on the furor came hours after a new ad aired. That ad was labeled as paid for by the U.S. government.The ad features video clips of Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussing the U.S. capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year."Nicolás Maduro had his chance ... until he didn't," Hegseth says in the ad. "He effed around and he found out." Another clip in the ad shows Rubio warning, "Don't play games with [President Trump] in office."The ads have been running in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election. Those contests will determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans will maintain their majorities in both chambers of Congress.The White House and MAGA Inc. did not immediately reply when asked whether the super PAC would cover the cost of the new ad or whether the buy had already been placed before Trump's announcement and would remain taxpayer-funded."The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday."This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.," Trump said.AdImpact has tracked roughly $9.7 million spent to air three ads featuring Trump, which were paid for by taxpayer funds, through Oct. 5. Trump's announcement that he would pay for the ads came three days after The New York Times, citing people familiar with the matter,  reported that "Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency."The Times said federal money to pay for the ads became available on Sept. 19, "when the Office of Management and Budget shifted $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds to a budget category called One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events." Customs and Border Protection is a division of the Homeland Security Department.Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., in a Sept. 24 letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, wrote, "The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates.'"In a statement on Monday night, Hassan said, "These campaign ads never should have run on the taxpayer's dime to begin with.""They were clearly wrong and clearly illegal, which is why the President should also immediately repay the taxpayers for the amount already spent on these ads," Hassan said. "There's a lesson here: We can't underestimate the difference that citizens can make in our country when they speak out and hold their leaders to account," she said.On Tuesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called for the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate the ads. "The government is not the President's campaign committee, and the Treasury is not his campaign account. The federal government has no legitimate business billing the public for campaign messaging that a candidate's political committee should pay for," Schumer wrote in a letter. Last week, the advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint urging the Federal Communications Commission, the Federal Trade Commission and TV broadcasters to stop airing the ads. Public Citizen previously asked the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate whether the ads violated federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act. That law restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns.MAGA Inc. has raised $424.4 million and spent $32.4 million during the 2025-26 cycle through Aug. 31, leaving the Trump Super PAC with $415.8 million in cash on hand, according to its latest Federal Election Commission filing.MAGA Inc. has spent at least $57 million this election cycle, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC filings, including $25 million in independent expenditures reported since the end of August.

schema.headline: Trump hedges on paying back government for ads that already aired

title: Mistral unveils new AI model it says rivals best open systems from China
description: Mistral on Tuesday unveiled a new AI model it said ranked among the best open models in the world, as Western companies race to close the capability g
body: Mistral on Tuesday unveiled a new AI model it said ranked among the best open models in the world, as Western companies race to close the capability gap with Chinese developers in the market.Mistral Large 4 (ML4), also known as le Chonk, is a 1-trillion-parameter model that is particularly effective at tasks related to cyber, coding, manufacturing, finance and multimodal, the French company said.Long considered Europe's only answer to OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral raised a 3 billion euros ($3.4 billion) Series D in September at a 21 billion euro valuation. The round cemented the company's status as one of the best-funded and most valuable AI startups in the region. Access to so-called open AI models — the most capable of which have been Chinese — has become a key flashpoint in the intensifying race for technological supremacy between the U.S. and China. Open AI models can be modified and self-hosted, in contrast to leading closed systems produced by OpenAI and Anthropic. Chinese open models are increasingly being adopted around the world.Mistral Large 4 is being launched in preview to developers and "cybersecurity leaders," alongside state authorities, before it is released more widely later this month, the company said.Rise of open modelsML4 was trained on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months that were deployed in Mistral's own data centers in Europe.When its core parameters are released, ML4 will rank among the top open-weight models globally on aggregate benchmark performance, Mistral said in a statement. The company added that ML4 was the strongest open-weight model developed outside China by a "substantial margin."The new model still lags behind the frontier in areas such as coding. "The model capabilities will further improve as we scale up our training capacity, following our Series D fundraise," said Guillaume Lample, co-founder and chief scientist of Mistral. "Further, the cyber defense capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyber attacks," he added.Open models were thrust into the spotlight earlier this year when it emerged that startup Hugging Face turned to Chinese-based Z.ai's GLM 5.2 to defend against a breach from rogue OpenAI agents. Hugging Face initially turned to leading U.S. closed systems to defend itself, but was blocked by guardrails that mistook its actions for an attack.Nvidia-backed American startup Reflection AI unveiled its first open model on Monday, which it claimed matched the capability of GLM 5.2, which was surpassed by GLM 5.3 in August.

schema.headline: Mistral unveils new AI model it says rivals best open systems from China

title: Kalshi launches transparency features on its election contracts ahead of midterms
description: Dado Ruvic | ReutersWith less than a month until midterms, Kalshi is launching three features on its election contracts to ensure traders have more tr
body: Dado Ruvic | ReutersWith less than a month until midterms, Kalshi is launching three features on its election contracts to ensure traders have more transparency on how active and accurate its markets are. First, the platform will provide tags that indicate which election markets are low volume, which Kalshi defines as those with less than $10,000. Prediction markets experts have warned prices in low-volume markets can fluctuate widely, while spreads between buying and selling can stretch. Second, Kalshi's own election markets will have Brier scores, which will measure the accuracy of the market's probabilities versus actual outcomes. Finally, the platform is launching an activity feeds feature, where it shows individual trades happening on election contracts live.  Kalshi decided to provide these transparency features after noting election traders were participating on markets covering local races over national ones. Kalshi's co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour called the midterms the "first meaningful prediction market election," noting the platform's election markets have grown six times faster than football markets this year, compared to the year before. Kalshi's internal data also indicates that more people are viewing their midterm markets than those who are trading by a ratio of five to one.In July, the prediction markets platform released a "Midterms Hub," which allows anyone to view traders' odds on markets tied to U.S. Senate and House of Representatives races. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Kalshi launches transparency features on its election contracts ahead of midterms

title: UBS CEO warns ‘hard measures’ are needed to tackle French debt crisis, as turmoil worsens
description: UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti has told CNBC that "hard measures" are needed to tackle France's spiraling debt crisis, warning that "small, incremental change
body: UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti has told CNBC that "hard measures" are needed to tackle France's spiraling debt crisis, warning that "small, incremental changes" will not be enough.Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk On The Street" on Tuesday, Ermotti compared the ongoing turmoil in Europe's bond market with the eurozone's sovereign debt crisis in 2011, warning that the size of France's economy means that its problems could be trickier to tackle this time round."We went through similar situations in the last 10 to 15 years in Spain, in Italy, in Greece, in Portugal," Ermotti said. "These countries that went into a big crisis are now the best performing countries in Europe."Other parts of Europe now facing a debt squeeze may now require "something similar" to "restore a credible path to growth".Asked if that meant austerity, Ermotti said: "It needs to go through hard measures… incremental small changes are not going to be enough to resolve the big debt pile."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconFrance 10-Year Bond.Yields on French government bonds — known as OATs — have jumped in recent weeks amid a broader sovereign debt sell-off in Europe, as investors grow increasingly concerned about the country's fiscal position.France's benchmark 10-year note yield stood at 4.7689% on Tuesday afternoon after easing 9 basis points. Borrowing costs are now higher in France than in Greece and Italy.Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen on Tuesday pledged huge spending cuts to get debt under control, warning that France ultimately risks defaulting on its debt.Mitch Reznick, head of cross-border credit at Federated Hermes, said in a Tuesday note that the country has quickly become the prime focus of the continent's bond woes, and suggested its debt is increasingly being priced "less like core Europe and more like the periphery."He added investors are abandoning French government bonds for quality in German Bunds, which is magnifying the spread between the two.Reznick said the European Central Bank remains unlikely to intervene at this point — but added that "its language could start to change" if spreads continue to gap out. "The OAT-Bund spread has moved above 140 basis points, as attention turns to France's high debt, large budget deficits, increased bond supply and political uncertainty ahead of the presidential election," said Reznick.

schema.headline: UBS CEO warns ‘hard measures’ are needed to tackle French debt crisis, as turmoil worsens

title: Emmy Awards leave broadcast TV for Prime Video in 2027 under six-year deal
description: An Emmy statue is seen on the red carpet ahead of the 74th Emmy Awards at the Microsoft Theater in Los Angeles, California, on Sept. 12, 2022.Chris De
body: An Emmy statue is seen on the red carpet ahead of the 74th Emmy Awards at the Microsoft Theater in Los Angeles, California, on Sept. 12, 2022.Chris Delmas | AFP | Getty ImagesThe Emmy Awards will leave its long-running broadcast network rotation for Amazon Prime Video in 2027 under a six-year exclusive global streaming deal, the e-commerce giant and the Television Academy announced on Tuesday. Under the agreement, Prime Video will stream the annual awards honoring the best in TV for free to all audiences, including nonsubscribers, in more than 240 countries and territories. Prime Video's rights to the Emmys will begin with the 2027 ceremony. NBC, owned by Comcast, aired the 2026 ceremony on Sept. 14. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. In the release, Prime Video was named as the "permanent home" for the Emmys, in contrast to the rotating agreement in place years prior.The switch ends the traditional "wheel-deal" setup to broadcast the awards, where ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox took turns hosting the Emmys each year. The system has been in place since at least 1994, with the most recent eight-year contract expiring this year. "Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Television Academy chair Cris Abrego said in a statement."Having a dedicated home with Prime Video allows us to build on that legacy with unprecedented global reach and a broader commitment to the Television Academy and our mission throughout the year," he said.The decision to move the 70-plus-year-old awards show to streaming reflects a broader trend in a shifting media landscape as Americans continue to ditch broadcast and cable TV for streaming service subscriptions. Streaming services have pushed further into live events in recent years, securing entertainment and sports rights alongside broadcast networks, and even winning rights that were previously exclusive to networks. In December 2025, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal with Alphabet's YouTube and YouTube TV for media rights to the Oscars, taking over from ABC in 2029. Netflix has exclusively aired the SAG Awards since 2024.

schema.headline: Emmy Awards leave broadcast TV for Prime Video in 2027 under six-year deal

title: DeepSeek considers doubling latest funding round to up to $15 billion, sources say
description: The DeepSeek Chinese AI company logo is seen in this photo illustration taken in Warsaw, Poland on 30 January, 2025.  Jaap Arriens | Nurphoto | Getty
body: The DeepSeek Chinese AI company logo is seen in this photo illustration taken in Warsaw, Poland on 30 January, 2025.  Jaap Arriens | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesChina's DeepSeek is considering expanding its latest funding round to as much as 100 billion yuan ($14.9 billion), double its earlier target, with state-backed funds and corporate investors jostling for stakes, people familiar with the matter told CNBC.The AI startup has fielded strong interest from state-backed funds, investment arms of listed Chinese companies and venture capital firms, according to the two people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to discuss the private talks.But DeepSeek is vetting prospective investors closely, turning away private investment funds raised from individual investors and limiting the pool largely to government and corporate funds, the people said.The company, which began taking outside capital for the first time this year, initially set a 50 billion yuan target for the current round.The fundraising process remains fluid, and the amount could still change before talks conclude, the people said. Bloomberg reported earlier Tuesday that DeepSeek is close to securing at least 80 billion yuan, with Tencent and battery maker CATL among the largest backers, and is eyeing an IPO in early 2027.CATL, Geely Auto and investment managers Monolith Management and Loyal Valley Capital have committed capital in the latest round, one of the people told CNBC.DeepSeek, CATL, Geely Auto, Monolith Management and Loyal Valley Capital did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. The round, initially expected to close by the end of August, has taken longer than planned as some prospective investors waver over the price, one of the people said, though talks are nearing the end. DeepSeek is seeking a valuation of about 500 billion yuan, or $75 billion, the people said. Its first external funding round, which closed in June, raised about 50 billion yuan. An investor filing related to the round implied a valuation of roughly 350 billion yuan.From lab to listing The AI startup triggered a sell-off in U.S. tech stocks in January 2025 after releasing AI models that rivaled American peers at far lower cost. Its latest model, V4.1 Flash, released in September, is designed for greater capability and faster inference, the company said.DeepSeek's decision to open up to external funding was seen as a sign of AI's ballooning capital demand and mounting pressure to retain talent amid intensifying competition. Founder Liang Wenfeng told investors at a private meeting in July that he prioritizes pushing the technology toward artificial general intelligence over maximizing profit.Talks on the current round were briefly suspended after Liang reportedly said in a private investor meeting that Chinese AI companies still lagged far behind their U.S. counterparts and relied heavily on Nvidia chips.DeepSeek has tapped CITIC Securities to prepare for a possible IPO on Shanghai's STAR Market, Reuters reported in September.Its domestic rival Moonshot AI is also reportedly targeting an early-2027 IPO after raising at a $50 billion valuation, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.

schema.headline: DeepSeek considers doubling latest funding round to up to $15 billion, sources say

title: This startup wants to reduce liquidation risk from margin calls on prediction markets
description: In this photo illustration, apps for online prediction market sites are shown on an electronic device on Feb. 25, 2026, in Chicago, Illinois.Scott Ols
body: In this photo illustration, apps for online prediction market sites are shown on an electronic device on Feb. 25, 2026, in Chicago, Illinois.Scott Olson | Getty ImagesStartup Edge Markets is building an automated system that allows institutions to authorize capital for prediction markets and helps companies move money to cover margin calls even when traditional banking systems are closed."Markets are becoming increasingly automated and global, but the infrastructure for accessing and moving capital on prediction markets falls short of real-world demand," said Seni Thomas, founder and CEO of Edge Markets. The company is a provider of financial infrastructure focused on the gaming and prediction markets industries.Edge Markets' new infrastructure, available through its Edge Pro service for market makers, aims to support institutional trading for markets that operate around the clock. It allows institutions to decide in advance how much capital to deploy, including setting limits on daily transactions executed by artificial intelligence agents and trading algorithms.The latest product comes as prediction market products face a roadblock: Perpetual futures — derivative contracts that never expire — trade nonstop, while traditional banking systems do not. Perpetuals were first launched by Kalshi in May 2026If a margin call happens outside of working hours, Edge's payment infrastructure, called Edge Connect, would allow institutional traders to pre-authorize a clearing house to automatically pull additional collateral. A margin call alerts a trader to add more funds if the trader's account drops below the required margin benchmark."Clearing houses should not have to tie up hundreds of millions of dollars simply because a margin call happens outside banking hours," Thomas said. "By allowing firms to establish permissions in advance, we can help reduce avoidable liquidations, improve capital efficiency and make always-on markets more resilient."The tool, which is expected to launch later this year, would help institutions route capital and transactions from trades to banks.Edge Markets is partnering with companies such as River Markets, ParlayX, OpenMarkets and Pikkit, whose clients will have access to the new product. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: This startup wants to reduce liquidation risk from margin calls on prediction markets

title: Rebounding oil exports through Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to stepped-up Iranian tanker attacks
description: watch nowIran has stepped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, threatening a fragile rebound of crude oil exports from the Persi
body: watch nowIran has stepped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, threatening a fragile rebound of crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf. Nearly 20 commercial ships, mostly tankers, have come under attack over the past month while sailing through Hormuz, the Persian Gulf or off the coast of Oman, according to the Joint Maritime Information Center, a group of U.S.-allied militaries that provide security updates to merchant vessels. Iran attacked roughly two ships for every 100 vessels that crossed the strait in the third quarter, said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, which tracks ships for defense departments and governments.Oil flows through Hormuz now depend on a major U.S. military commitment to protect tankers transiting along a southern route along the coast of Oman.With the security situation in Hormuz still dangerous, it is unclear how long the rebound in crude exports can be sustained in the absence of a negotiated settlement or capitulation by Tehran. Shuttle systemIn many cases, tankers are bringing crude through Hormuz and then transferring the oil onto ships in the Gulf of Oman that haul it to Asia. This shuttle system reduces the exposure to attack from Iran but also requires more vessels to move the oil. "Nobody in Washington thinks this is sustainable financially," said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush, referring to the U.S. military commitment in the Gulf, ship-to-ship transfers and heightened tanker rates. "It's an inefficient way to move commodities, not just oil, out of Hormuz," McNally said.Crude oil shipments through Hormuz fluctuate daily, sometimes matching or even exceeding levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler, a firm that tracks tankers and global trade flows. At other times, exports are lower than volumes seen before the conflict. Shipments averaged about 10.3 million barrels per day for the week ended Saturday, about 23% below a prewar baseline of 13.5 million bpd, according to Kpler data published Monday.Windward estimates crude through Hormuz is averaging 9-10 million bpd compared with a prewar baseline of 14.5 million bpd. While crude flows are volatile, they have ramped up compared with earlier in the war as the U.S. military has successfully carved out the shipping route along Oman's coast, analysts say. High costsBut shippers are ferrying crude through Hormuz at high cost to the lives of their crews and in freight and insurance rates, Bockmann said. Since July, at least nine sailors have died, 18 injured and three are missing, according to the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations agency."Volumes are getting through but they're getting through at a time of extremely high maritime risk," Bockmann said. As security has deteriorated, the cost of shipping crude from the Persian Gulf to China has skyrocketed to $1 million per day for each tanker. "Oil flows have recovered because the market participants have accepted greater operational complexity and higher costs," said Richard Meade, editor in chief of Lloyd's List, a London-based maritime industry trade publication, in a briefing last Thursday. But the threat to tankers remains the same, Meade said. Brent oil prices, the international benchmark, are still hovering near $100 per barrel, even as more crude makes it out of Hormuz. "If the market believed that this was sustainable, I think you would be seeing much lower prices," McNally at Rapidan said. Prices remain high because "it's still costly to deliver and insure and land crude in consuming regions where benchmark prices are set," he said.  And while more oil is getting out, freedom of navigation in Hormuz has not been restored, McNally said. Tehran continues to insist that it controls the strait. Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Monday hailed down a tanker transiting the strait and ordered the ship to turn around or face attack, according to an incident report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre. The vessel complied."The oil market is not becoming more secure," Meade said. "It is becoming more efficient at operating under sustained insecurity."

schema.headline: Rebounding oil exports through Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to stepped-up Iranian tanker attacks

title: Trade deficit hits $105.6 billion, widest since just before Trump tariffs enacted last year
description: Trucks move goods in a shipping container next to large stacks of shipping containers and cranes at the Port of Long Beach  Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026.
body: Trucks move goods in a shipping container next to large stacks of shipping containers and cranes at the Port of Long Beach  Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Allen J. Schaben | Los Angeles Times | Getty ImagesThe U.S. trade deficit widened sharply in August amid an influx of goods related to the artificial intelligence build-out and the vagaries of import tariffs, the Commerce Department reported Tuesday.Imports swelled 4.3% for the month, pushing the total imbalance to $105.6 billion. That marked a 13.7% jump from July and was ahead of the Dow Jones consensus estimate for $102 billion.It also was the steepest deficit since the all-time gap in March 2025, recorded just before President Donald Trump's "liberation day" announcement of "reciprocal" tariffs against U.S. trading partners.Though the monthly total was up, the year-to-date deficit of $138.2 billion was off nearly 20% from the same period a year ago. "Rising prices overstate the moves, but nonetheless net trade is set to drag on Q3 GDP growth," said Oren Klachkin, financial economist at Nationwide. "We see this as a sign of strong domestic demand, not economic weakness."Imports as a rule generally subtract from gross domestic product calculations. However, if the imports reflect stronger demand and consumption, they can be offset elsewhere.Nevertheless, Goldman Sachs cut its tracking estimate for third-quarter economic growth to 3.1%, down 0.3 percentage point from its prior estimate. The Atlanta Federal Reserve's GDPNow tracker lowered its estimate to 3.7% following the trade report, down 0.1 percentage point from the last update.watch now

schema.headline: Trade deficit hits $105.6 billion, widest since just before Trump tariffs enacted last year
